name: Chloe Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on twelve-hour shifts at the copper pit, four days on, four off. I'm up at four, on the bus by five, and in the seat of a 240-tonne haul truck by half past six, running ore from the shovel up the ramp to the crusher. These days I spend half my shift training the new drivers, sitting in the buddy seat and telling them to stop riding the brakes on the downhill. What wears me out isn't the driving, it's the dust and the night shifts, which get harder every year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and what do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-one years this March. I started on water carts when there were hardly any women on site, and I'm one of the senior operators now, plus I've been the union delegate for our crew for twelve years. What I like is the crew, honestly. Rosa, who I trained, eats lunch with me every day in the crib room, and when someone's kid is sick the whole shift knows about it by the morning break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Every couple of years some salesman comes through with a new system that's going to change everything, and we end up with another screen in the cab that beeps at us. I'd say it at the union meeting and I'd say it in the crib room, but I don't post anything online, I've never seen the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief. I've got maybe three or four years left before I hang up the keys, and I'd like them to look like the last thirty. My husband Marwan and I have the house paid off and a good bit put away, so if nothing changes, nothing changes for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep driving, keep training the young ones, and keep pushing the company on the night shift roster, which is the real fight right now. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff, I don't use it now and I wouldn't start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday. Maybe a bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about AI at the mine right now that bothers you, even in this quiet version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fatigue cameras in the cab. They watch your eyes and if you blink too long the seat shakes and a supervisor gets a message. I understand why, but I've driven these roads for thirty years and I don't like being graded by a camera that doesn't know me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the new drivers you train, if this is how it goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the haul roads properly, because a good driver saves tyres and fuel and nobody's machine does that yet. Tyres on those trucks cost more than my first house. That's still the skill that keeps you employed.

S0.say: I'd tell the crew and the union meeting that it was mostly salesman talk, as I always said. I'd say it in person, not online, because I never post anything.
S0.think: Privately it would be a relief to finish my last three or four years the way I spent the first thirty. With the house paid off and savings put away, nothing changes for us.
S0.do: Keeps driving and training new operators exactly as now. Keeps pushing the company on the night shift roster through the union and stays away from AI tools.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, as if it were any ordinary day.
S0.quote: Tyres on those trucks cost more than my first house. That's still the skill that keeps you employed.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe measures every change against thirty-one years in the seat, and AI talk sounds to her like another round of salesmen. Even in the quietest picture she brought up the fatigue cameras, so being watched by machines already bothers her. Her union role is clearly central to who she is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need it in the contract, full stop. If tasks are getting taken over, the union needs a say in which ones and what happens to the people doing them. I'd say that at every meeting until people got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my last few years get messier. I know they'll go after the haul trucks first, because the company down the valley already runs driverless ones and they don't need breaks. I'll probably be fine, but I'd spend those years watching younger people like Rosa get shuffled around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to push for a clause that nobody loses a job to a new system without a retraining offer and proper notice, at least six months. I'd keep driving and training as long as they let me. If they asked me to learn to run the trucks from a control room, I'd probably say no and take the package instead, because I'm too old to sit in front of screens all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my own money, we're all right. More that the place I've given my working life to would start feeling like somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned taking a package. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it a year or two early rather than learning a new job at fifty-nine. With my savings and my pension we'd manage, and Marwan's been on at me to slow down anyway. But I'd hate leaving the crew while the fight's still going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The middle ones, people in their forties with mortgages and kids at school. The young ones can retrain and the old ones like me can go. It's the ones in between who'd get squeezed hardest.

S1.say: I'd tell everyone at work that automation has to go into the union contract, with a say over which tasks go and what happens to the people. I'd keep repeating it until people got sick of hearing it.
S1.think: Privately I know the haul trucks will be first, because a site down the valley already runs driverless ones. My own money is safe, but my last years would be spent watching younger people like Rosa get moved around.
S1.do: Pushes the union for a clause guaranteeing six months' notice and a retraining offer before anyone loses a job to a new system. Keeps driving while allowed, and would take an early package rather than move to a control room job.
S1.feel: Uneasy, less about money than about her workplace turning into somewhere she doesn't recognise.
S1.quote: It's the ones in between who'd get squeezed hardest.
S1.fieldNote: Her first move is collective, not personal: she reaches for the union contract before thinking about herself. She would rather leave early than learn a screen job, which shows her resistance to change is real even with money to fall back on. Her worry lands on workers in their forties, not on herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the bosses and the tech people doing whatever they want while governments sit on their hands. I'd say it loudly, and I'd want the union to say it louder. Two years isn't enough time for anyone to protect anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I'd be sixty by then and I could stop. But I'd be stopping because a machine pushed me out, not because I chose to, and that matters to me. And the town would be gutted. Half the main street lives off mine wages, from the bakery to the tyre shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union executive and push for a campaign, a public one, for the government to force the companies to pay into a fund for every job they cut. I'd go to the protests, which I've done before, over safety. Then I'd probably retire in the first year rather than fight to sit in a truck that doesn't need me, and I'd keep working with the union as a volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my stomach turn. I'm not scared for our money. I'm angry, and sad for the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change things for you, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no time for the union to bargain anything. In the slow one we'd get a few contracts in, a few clauses, notice periods. With two years, the company just announces it and we're arguing after the fact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you could stop. What would retiring like that actually feel like on the day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep picturing handing in my lamp and my access card at the gate, and some young fellow in a hi-vis vest just scanning it and nodding. Thirty-three years by then, and the last thing I hand over is a plastic card. I'd go home and probably cry in the car before I went inside.

S2.say: I'd say the bosses and the tech companies are doing whatever they like while governments sit on their hands. I'd want the union to say it even louder, because two years is no time to protect anyone.
S2.think: Privately I could afford to stop at sixty, but I'd be pushed out by a machine rather than choosing to go. What really gets me is the town, because half the main street lives off mine wages.
S2.do: Pushes the union executive for a public campaign demanding that companies pay into a fund for every job cut, and joins protests. Retires within the first year and keeps volunteering for the union.
S2.feel: Angry and sad for her town, with a turning stomach, though not afraid about her own money.
S2.quote: Thirty-three years by then, and the last thing I hand over is a plastic card.
S2.fieldNote: Her savings take the edge off, but this picture still gets to her because it takes away the one tool she trusts, which is bargaining over time. She blames employers and weak governments directly. The image of handing in her access card was the most emotional moment so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same line as before, but I'd say we've got a few years and no excuse to waste them. I'd tell people at the union meeting that this is the time to get things written down, before the robots turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is past when I'd planned to retire, so for me it's mostly about the people I leave behind. I'd be sixty-three by 2031. I'd want to leave knowing the union got something solid in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on another two or three years, partly to be at the bargaining table for the next enterprise agreement, which is due in 2028. I'd push for redundancy pay to be doubled for anyone cut by automation, and for the company to fund retraining at the technical college in town. Then I'd retire around 2029 on my own terms, not theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's something to hold onto. I'd have a job to do before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys one more round of bargaining. That's the difference between a protest and a contract. A contract actually protects people after I've gone home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go near any of the new technology in those years, to understand what you're fighting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Rosa can do that, she's good with it. I'd rather spend my time on the people, and let the ones with the phones tell me what the machines are doing.

S3.say: I'd tell the union that a few years' warning leaves no excuse to waste time. We'd need to get protections written down before the robots arrive.
S3.think: Five years takes me past my planned retirement, so it's mostly about the people I leave behind. I'd want to go knowing the union locked in something solid.
S3.do: Stays on two or three more years to sit at the 2028 bargaining table, pushing for doubled redundancy pay and company-funded retraining at the local college. Retires around 2029 on her own timing.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but steadied by having one last job to finish before she goes.
S3.quote: It buys one more round of bargaining. That's the difference between a protest and a contract.
S3.fieldNote: For Chloe the value of time is measured in bargaining rounds, which is a very specific and telling way to see it. She still refuses to engage with the technology and is happy to hand that to younger colleagues. Five years turns her from angry into purposeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decade to get it right, so governments had better use it. Proper retraining, proper pensions, and the companies paying their share. I'd say it at the union and I'd say it to our local member of parliament if I got the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's after I've gone. I'd be sixty-eight by 2036, out of the pit and probably minding grandchildren. It's my grandkids I'd think about, what work there'll be for them in a town built around a hole in the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire when I'd planned to, around sixty-one or sixty-two. Before that, I'd make sure there's someone ready to take over as delegate, probably Rosa. After I retire, I'd stay in the retired members' group and write letters to the local paper, which I've always threatened to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for myself. A bit of a heavy feeling when I think about the grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren about work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Leila's boy is seven and he wants to drive trucks like his nanna. I'd tell him to learn to fix things and to look after people, because somebody will still have to do both. I wouldn't tell him to come to the mine, and that breaks my heart a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hand over to Rosa. Does she know that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. She'd laugh at me. But she's the only one on the crew who'd stand up to a manager and also understand the computers, and you need both now.

S4.say: I'd say a decade gives governments time to get it right, with proper retraining, pensions and companies paying their share. I'd say it at the union and to our local member of parliament.
S4.think: For me it's after I've retired, so my thoughts go to my grandchildren. I'd wonder what work there will be for them in a town built around a hole in the ground.
S4.do: Retires as planned around 61 or 62, first preparing Rosa to take over as union delegate. Stays in the retired members' group and writes letters to the local paper.
S4.feel: Calm for herself, with a heavy feeling when she thinks about her grandchildren.
S4.quote: I wouldn't tell him to come to the mine, and that breaks my heart a bit.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her own position is safe and her concern moves to the next generation. Admitting she would steer her grandson away from the mine was a quiet but big moment for someone whose life is built on it. She also admits that the next delegate will need computer skills she has chosen not to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no question. Not for me, I'll be fine, but because nobody gets time to bargain. What would help is a law that makes companies give real notice and pay into a fund for every job a machine takes, and a government with the spine to enforce it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women. I was one of three women on site when I started, and now there are dozens of us driving trucks. Driving is the job that let women into mining, and it's the first one they'll automate. Somebody should be counting that.

headlineQuote: Driving is the job that let women into mining, and it's the first one they'll automate.
portrait: Chloe Haddad is a 58-year-old senior haul truck operator and union delegate at a copper pit, with thirty-one years on site and a paid-off house. She avoids new technology, has never used AI, and would rather retire than learn to run trucks from a screen. Her savings mean she is never worried about money, so her concern goes to the crew, the town and her grandchildren. She moves from calm in AI Plateau to anxious and angry in AGI by 2028, and judges the slower pictures by how many rounds of union bargaining they would allow. She blames employers and weak governments, and reaches first for collective action.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time for the union to bargain protections for workers.
whatWouldHelp: A law forcing companies to give real notice and pay into a fund for every job lost to automation, enforced by a government willing to act.
